sections.text:
1 Cf. supra p. 124, n. 2.
2 Hoc excerptum duobus partibus constare videtur, quae laxe inter se coniunctae
sunt. Prior praebet thema mundi, ab eis quae apud Firmicum III, 1 et Paulum
Alex. (R. Ὅπως ἐστὶν ἡ τοῦ κόσμου γένεσις) inveniuntur omnino diversum. Iam
antiqui Chaldaei mundi genituram determinaverunt, si excerpto anonymo a
cardinale Pitra (Analect. sacra, V, 300) edito fidere licet (cf. supra, p. 113).
In altera parte chorographia quam vocamus astrologica exponitur, i. e. regiones
terrae enumerantur singulis planetis vel zodiaci signis subiectae. Talia iam graecos
docuisse omnibus notum est et iam in Catal. Veneto (p. 84 ss.) de auctoribus huius
divisionis egimus (cf. et infra cod. Neap. 19, f. 379v). Illa praecepta Arabes quoque
et Persae ad plagas terrarum quas incolebant accomodasse, vel ex excerptis libro-
rum nostrorum graecorum perspicuum est (vide e. g. Achmetis collectanea in
cod. Venet. 5, f. 225-225v = cod. Angelic. 29, f. 165, et ipsius Apomasaris lib. III,
cap. κβ' in cod. Flor. 11, f. 159 = cod. Angelic., f. 77). Frequenter autem similia in
Orientalibus libris inveniri certiorem me fecit litteris, qua semper est et humani-
tate et scientia, Theodorus Nöldeke. Nempe accurata enumeratio regionum secun-
dum ordinem septem climatum vel septem planetarum et deinde duodecim
signorum zodiaci invenitur in praestantissimo lexico geographi Iâqût (I 29-36).
Breviorem descriptionem praebet Mas'ûdi (Les prairies d'or, I, p. 181-2).
Mandaei quoque huiusmodi studiis vacuerunt : in collectaneis astrologicis
inscriptis Asfar Malwâšê (= Liber signorum zodiaci, cod. Petermann 155 (Berlin)
cap. 123 ss.) chorographia inserta est ex Arabico exemplari versa et depravata. —
Idem Theodorus Nöldeke ad nomina geographica, quae Apomasaris interpres
sections.en:
1 Compare above p. 124, n. 2.
2 This excerpt seems to consist of two parts, which are loosely joined together
between themselves. The first provides the theme of the world, entirely different from those which are found in Firmicus III, 1 and Paulus
Alexandrinus (R. Ὅπως ἐστὶν ἡ τοῦ κόσμου γένεσις ('How the genesis of the world is')). Already
the ancient Chaldeans determined the geniture of the world, if one may trust the anonymous excerpt edited by
Cardinal Pitra (Analect. sacra, V, 300) (compare above, p. 113).
In the other part the chorography which we call astrological is set forth, that is, the regions
of the earth are enumerated as subjected to individual planets or signs of the zodiac. That the Greeks already taught such things
is known to all and already in the Catal. Veneto (p. 84 ff.) we have discussed the authors of this
division (compare also below cod. Neap. 19, f. 379v). That the Arabs and Persians also adapted those precepts
to the regions of the lands which they inhabited, is clear even from the excerpts of our Greek
books (see for example the collectanea of Achmet in
cod. Venet. 5, f. 225-225v = cod. Angelic. 29, f. 165, and book III of Apomasar himself,
ch. κβ' ('22') in cod. Flor. 11, f. 159 = cod. Angelic., f. 77). Moreover, that similar things are frequently found in
Oriental books I was informed by letter, with the humanity and knowledge which he always possesses,
by Theodor Nöldeke. Indeed an accurate enumeration of regions according
to the order of the seven climates or seven planets and then of the twelve
signs of the zodiac is found in the most excellent lexicon of the geographer Yāqūt (I 29-36).
A shorter description is provided by Mas'udi (Les prairies d'or, I, p. 181-2).
The Mandaeans also devoted themselves to studies of this kind: in the astrological collectanea
entitled Asfar Malwâšê (= Book of the signs of the zodiac, cod. Petermann 155 (Berlin)
ch. 123 ff.) a chorography is inserted, translated and corrupted from an Arabic exemplar. —

summary.headline: Dog Star Omens and World Horoscope
summary.text: Astrological omens for the rising of the Dog Star, with weather, harvest, disease, animal mortality, and maritime predictions assigned to days of Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn. A world horoscope follows, placing the Ascendant in Cancer with Jupiter, Saturn in Libra, and the lunar nodes in Gemini and Sagittarius; the commentary discusses astrological chorography and authorities including Firmicus, Paulus Alexandrinus, Achmet, Apomasar, Yāqūt, Mas'udi, and Theodor Nöldeke.
